      <content name="title"><span class="qt2">Cervical</span> <span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">Cancer</span></span></content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="FullSummary">What is <span class="qt2">cervical</span> <span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">cancer</span></span>?<p><span class="qt2">Cervical</span> <span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">cancer is cancer</span></span> that starts in the cells of the <span class="qt2">cervix. The cervix</span> is part of the female reproductive system. It is the lower, narrow end of the <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">uterus (womb</span></span>), which opens into the vagina (birth canal).</p><p><span class="qt2">Cervical</span> <span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">cancer</span></span> usually develops slowly. Before <span class="qt2">cervical</span> cells become <span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">cancer</span></span>, they start to look abnormal. These cells are called "precancers." If they aren't destroyed or removed, they may become <span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">cancer</span></span> cells that grow out of control and spread to other parts of your body.</p><p>Screening tests for <span class="qt2">cervical</span> <span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">cancer</span></span> can help find abnormal cells so you can get treatment to prevent <span class="qt2">cervical</span> <span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">cancer</span></span>. These tests can also find <span class="qt2">cervical</span> <span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">cancer</span></span> early when it's usually easier to treat.</p>What causes <span class="qt2">cervical</span> <span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">cancer</span></span>?<p>Almost all <span class="qt2">cervical</span> <span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">cancers</span></span> are caused by a long-lasting infection with a virus called human papillomavirus (HPV). There are many types of HPV. The types that cause <span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">cancer</span></span> are called "high-risk HPV." High-risk HPV is very common. It can be passed from one person to another through close skin-to-skin touching, usually during vaginal, anal, or oral sex. Most people who are infected have no symptoms and don't know they have it.</p><p>If you're infected with high-risk HPV, usually your immune system will get rid of it within a year or two. But if your immune system can't control the infection, it may last for many years. Over time, HPV can turn normal <span class="qt2">cervical</span> cells into abnormal cells. Without treatment, these cells may keep changing until they become <span class="qt2">cervical</span> <span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">cancer</span></span>.</p>Who is more likely to develop <span class="qt2">cervical</span> <span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">cancer</span></span>?<p><span class="qt2">Cervical</span> <span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">cancer</span></span> is most common in people over age 30. If you have a high-risk HPV infection in your <span class="qt2">cervix</span>, you're more likely to develop <span class="qt2">cervical</span> <span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">cancer</span></span> if you:</p><ul><li>Have a weakened immune system because you:
	<ul><li>Have a disease that harms your immune system, such as HIV.</li><li>Take medicine to control your immune system, such as certain medicines to treat <span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">cancer</span></span> or autoimmune diseases</li></ul>
</li><li>Smoke tobacco or breathe secondhand smoke.</li><li>Use birth control pills or have given birth to many children.</li><li>Have obesity.</li><li>Were exposed to a medicine called DES (diethylstilbestrol) before you were born. Between 1940-1971, DES was sometimes prescribed during pregnancy to prevent miscarriages. DES was later linked to health problems, including <span class="qt2">cervical</span> <span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">cancer</span></span>.</li></ul>What are the symptoms of <span class="qt2">cervical</span> <span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">cancer</span></span>?<p><span class="qt2">Cervical</span> <span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">cancer</span></span> usually doesn't cause symptoms when it first starts to grow. But when it does cause symptoms, they may include:</p><ul><li>Vaginal bleeding that's not normal for you, such as bleeding after sex or between menstrual periods</li><li>Vaginal discharge (fluid) that's watery and has a strong odor or contains blood</li><li>Pelvic pain or pain during sex</li></ul><p>If <span class="qt2">cervical</span> <span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">cancer</span></span> spreads to other parts of your body, symptoms may include:</p><ul><li>Unusual vaginal bleeding or discharge</li><li>Pelvic pain or pain during sex</li><li>Difficult or painful bowel movements (poops) or bleeding from the rectum when having a bowel movement</li><li>Difficult or painful urination (peeing) or blood in your urine (pee)</li><li>Dull backache</li><li>Swollen legs</li><li>Abdominal (belly) pain</li><li>Fatigue</li></ul>How is <span class="qt2">cervical</span> <span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">cancer</span></span> diagnosed?<p>If you have symptoms or had an abnormal result on a screening test for <span class="qt2">cervical</span> <span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">cancer</span></span>, your health care provider will do more tests to find out if you have <span class="qt2">cervical</span> <span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">cancer</span></span>. They will:</p><ul><li>Ask about your medical history and your family health history</li><li>Do a pelvic exam</li><li>Suggest tests to diagnose or rule out <span class="qt2">cervical</span> <span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">cancer</span></span>, including: 
	<ul><li>Colposcopy, a procedure using a device called a colposcope, which helps your provider examine your <span class="qt2">cervix</span> for abnormal areas</li><li><span class="qt2">Cervical</span> biopsy, a procedure to remove a tissue sample from your <span class="qt2">cervix</span> so that it can be examined under a microscope to look for signs of <span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">cancer</span></span>. Most biopsies can be done in your provider's office</li></ul>
</li></ul>What are the treatments for <span class="qt2">cervical</span> <span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">cancer</span></span>?<p>Different treatments are available for <span class="qt2">cervical</span> <span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">cancer</span></span>. The best treatment for you depends on your health, how much <span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">cancer</span></span> you have, whether it has spread, and which treatment you prefer. You may have more than one treatment, including:</p><ul><li>Surgery to remove the <span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">cancer</span></span>.</li><li>Radiation therapy, which uses high-energy x-rays or other types of radiation to kill <span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">cancer</span></span> cells or keep them from growing. The therapy may use radiation from a machine, or a radioactive substance may be placed in your body near the <span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">cancer</span></span>.</li><li>Chemotherapy (chemo), which uses special medicines to shrink or kill the <span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">cancer</span></span>. The medicine may be pills, or it may be given through a vein (by IV). Sometimes, both types of chemo are used.</li><li>Targeted therapy, which uses special medicines to block the growth and spread of <span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">cancer</span></span> cells.</li><li>Immunotherapy, which helps your immune system fight <span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">cancer</span></span> cells.</li></ul>Can <span class="qt2">cervical</span> <span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">cancer</span></span> be prevented?<p>Almost all <span class="qt2">cervical</span> <span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">cancer</span></span> can be prevented by:</p><ul><li>HPV vaccination. HPV vaccines provide the most protection if you get them before you're exposed to HPV. So, it's best to get vaccinated before you become sexually active.  Medical experts recommend vaccinating children between ages 9 and 12.</li><li>Routine <span class="qt2">cervical</span> <span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">cancer</span></span> screening. Two types of screening tests may be part of your routine health checkup. Both tests use a sample of <span class="qt2">cervical</span> cells that your provider collects with a swab: 
	<ul><li>A Pap smear checks for abnormal cells so they can be treated before they become <span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">cancer</span></span></li><li>An HPV test checks for high-risk HPV infections that can cause <span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">cancer</span></span>.</li></ul>
</li><li>Getting the right follow-up treatment if a screening test finds abnormal cells and/or high-risk HPV.</li></ul><p>You can lower your risk for <span class="qt2">cervical</span> <span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">cancer</span></span> by not smoking. Using condoms correctly during sex lowers your risk of getting an HPV infection, but doesn't prevent it completely.  Condom use has been linked to fewer cases of <span class="qt2">cervical</span> <span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">cancer</span></span>. If you or your partner is allergic to latex, you can use polyurethane condoms.</p><p>NIH: National <span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">Cancer</span></span> Institute</p></content>

      <content name="title">Women's Health Checkup</content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Pelvic Exam</content>
      <content name="FullSummary"><p>Regular checkups with your health care provider are different from appointments for sickness or injury. Your checkups, which are also called well-woman exams, include physical exams as well as preventive care. They can help find health problems early, when they may be easier to treat.</p><p>Your checkup is usually done by a provider with special training in caring for women. It will include screenings for chronic diseases. As a woman, you may also get special exams and screenings, such as:</p><ul><li>A pelvic exam to check the health of your reproductive organs. Your provider will look at your vulva, vagina, and <span class="qt2">cervix</span>. They will also do an internal exam to feel the size and shape of your internal organs such as the <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">uterus</span></span> and ovaries.</li><li>A <span class="qt2">cervical</span> <span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">cancer</span></span> screening, which uses a Pap test, an HPV test, or both. The tests can help prevent <span class="qt2">cervical</span> <span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">cancer</span></span>.  A Pap test checks for <span class="qt2">cervical</span> <span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">cancer</span></span> and for abnormal cells that could turn into <span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">cancer</span></span>. An HPV test looks for the types of HPV which can cause <span class="qt2">cervical</span> <span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">cancer</span></span>. For both tests, your provider will take a sample of cells from the surface of your <span class="qt2">cervix</span> and send them to a lab to be examined under a microscope.</li><li>A clinical breast exam to check for breast <span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">cancer</span></span>. Your provider will feel and look at your breasts and armpit area for lumps or other changes. They may also recommend a mammogram, which is an x-ray picture of your breast.</li></ul><p>Which tests you get and how often you need them will depend on your age, overall health, and family health history. In some cases, your provider may also recommend other tests as well. For example, if you have a family history of certain <span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">cancers</span></span>, your provider may recommend genetic testing.</p><p>During your checkup, you and your provider may also talk about other issues, such as:</p><ul><li>Birth control or family planning</li><li>Menopause</li><li>Menstrual concerns</li><li>Sexually transmitted infections (STIs)</li><li>Vaccines</li><li>Your overall physical health and mental well-being, including suggestions on how to have a healthy lifestyle</li></ul><p>To make the most of your next checkup, bring a list of any questions or concerns you have, so you can talk about them with your provider.</p></content>

      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="FullSummary">What is <span class="qt2">cervical</span> <span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">cancer</span></span> screening?<p><span class="qt2">Cervical</span> <span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">cancer is cancer</span></span> that starts in the cells of the <span class="qt2">cervix. The cervix</span> is part of the female reproductive system. It is the lower, narrow end of the <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">uterus (womb</span></span>), which opens into the vagina (birth canal). <span class="qt2">Cervical</span> <span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">cancer</span></span> screening is an important part of routine health care for people who have a <span class="qt2">cervix</span>.</p><p><span class="qt2">Cervical</span> <span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">cancer</span></span> screening tests look for <span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">cancer</span></span> before you have any symptoms. <span class="qt2">Cervical</span> <span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">cancer</span></span> usually develops slowly. Before <span class="qt2">cervical</span> cells become <span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">cancer</span></span>, they start to look abnormal. These cells are called "precancers". If they aren't destroyed or removed, they may become <span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">cancer</span></span> cells that grow out of control and spread to other parts of your body.</p><p>Screening can help find abnormal cells so you can get treatment to prevent <span class="qt2">cervical</span> <span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">cancer</span></span>. These tests can also help to find <span class="qt2">cervical</span> <span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">cancer</span></span> early when it's usually easier to treat.</p>What tests screen for <span class="qt2">cervical</span> <span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">cancer</span></span>?<p><span class="qt2">Cervical</span> <span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">cancer</span></span> screening is usually part of a woman's health checkup during a pelvic exam. These tests use a sample of <span class="qt2">cervical</span> cells that your health care provider collects with a swab:</p><ul><li>A Pap test  (also called a Pap smear or <span class="qt2">cervical</span> cytology) checks for abnormal cells so they can be treated before they become <span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">cancer</span></span>.</li><li>An HPV (human papillomavirus) test checks for certain HPV infections that can cause <span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">cancer</span></span>. HPV is a group of viruses that spread through sexual contact. The types that cause <span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">cancer</span></span> are called "high-risk HPV."</li><li>The HPV/Pap cotest uses an HPV and Pap test together to check for both high-risk HPV and <span class="qt2">cervical</span> cell changes.</li></ul><p>If your screening tests are abnormal, your provider may do more tests, such as a biopsy. How often you should be screened for <span class="qt2">cervical</span> <span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">cancer</span></span> and which tests you should get will depend on your age and health history.</p>What are the possible benefits and harms of <span class="qt2">cervical</span> <span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">cancer</span></span> screening?<p><span class="qt2">Cervical</span> <span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">cancer</span></span> screening saves lives. Screening can detect <span class="qt2">cervical</span> changes early, lowering your chance of dying from <span class="qt2">cervical</span> <span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">cancer</span></span>. But, <span class="qt2">cervical</span> <span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">cancer</span></span> screening has potential harms.</p><p>The possible harms of <span class="qt2">cervical</span> <span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">cancer</span></span> screening include:</p><p>The results can sometimes be wrong.</p><ul><li>Getting a false-positive result means that your test results appear abnormal, but there are no precancerous or cancerous cells. A false-positive may lead to: 
	<ul><li>Worry while you have more tests to look for signs of <span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">cancer</span></span>.</li><li>Follow-up tests or treatment that you may not have needed.</li></ul>
</li><li>Getting a false-negative result means that your test results appear normal, but there are precancer or cancerous cells. A false-negative may lead to: 
	<ul><li>You may delay seeking treatment even if you have symptoms.</li></ul>
</li></ul>Should I be screened for <span class="qt2">cervical</span> <span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">cancer</span></span>?<p>Talk with your provider about how often you should be screened for <span class="qt2">cervical</span> <span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">cancer</span></span> and which tests you should get. This will depend on your age and health history. If you have a <span class="qt2">cervix</span>, it's recommended that you have your first Pap smear at age 21 and begin screening with an HPV test at age 25. You may need screening more often if you:</p><ul><li>Had an abnormal HPV test, Pap smear, or <span class="qt2">cervical</span> biopsy in the recent past.</li><li>Have had a diagnosis of <span class="qt2">cervical</span> <span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">cancer</span></span>.</li><li>Have a weakened immune system.</li><li>Were exposed to a drug called DES (Diethylstilbestrol) before you were born. Between the years 1940-1971, DES was sometimes prescribed to prevent miscarriages.</li></ul><p>If you are over age 65 and have had regular Pap smear screenings with normal results, your provider may tell you that you no longer need them. If you have HIV, you may need to continue screenings after age 65.</p><p>You don't need <span class="qt2">cervical</span> <span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">cancer</span></span> screening if you had a total <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">hysterectomy</span></span> (surgery to remove your <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">uterus</span></span> and <span class="qt2">cervix</span>) because of a condition that was not <span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">cancer</span></span>. But if your <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">hysterectomy</span></span> was related to <span class="qt2">cervical</span> <span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">cancer</span></span> or precancer, ask your provider whether you need screening.</p><p>NIH: National <span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">Cancer</span></span> Institute</p></content>

    <document rank="3" url="https://medlineplus.gov/cervixdisorders.html">
      <content name="title"><span class="qt2">Cervix</span> Disorders</content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle"><span class="qt2">Cervical</span> Dysplasia</content>
      <content name="altTitle"><span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">Uterine</span></span> <span class="qt2">Cervix</span> Disorders</content>
      <content name="FullSummary">What is a <span class="qt2">cervix</span> disorder?<p>A <span class="qt2">cervix</span> disorder is a problem with your <span class="qt2">cervix. The cervix</span> is part of the female reproductive system. It is the lower, narrow end of the <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">uterus (womb</span></span>), which opens into the vagina (birth canal). The <span class="qt2">cervix</span> has a small opening that expands during childbirth. It also allows menstrual blood to leave your body.</p><p>You may not have any symptoms of a <span class="qt2">cervix</span> disorder, but routine pelvic exams and a Pap smear test  can help determine if you may need treatment.</p><p><span class="qt2">Cervix</span> disorders can include:</p><ul><li><span class="qt2">Cervical</span> <span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">cancer is a cancer</span></span> that starts in the cells of the <span class="qt2">cervix</span>.</li><li>Cervicitis is swelling of the <span class="qt2">cervix</span>. An infection usually causes it, but it can also be caused by skin irritation. Treatment can help you avoid potential complications like pelvic inflammatory disease (PID).</li><li><span class="qt2">Cervical</span> incompetence (also called <span class="qt2">cervical</span> insufficiency) can happen during pregnancy. The opening of your <span class="qt2">cervix</span> widens too early. This may cause you to give birth too soon, or you could lose the fetus.</li><li><span class="qt2">Cervical</span> polyps and cysts are fleshy or fluid-filled growths on your <span class="qt2">cervix</span>. These growths are usually benign (not <span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">cancer</span></span>). They are more common during your reproductive years, especially after age 20.</li></ul>Who is more likely to develop <span class="qt2">cervix</span> disorders?<p>You are more likely to develop a <span class="qt2">cervix</span> disorder if:</p><ul><li>You've had a previous <span class="qt2">cervical</span> procedure or surgery.</li><li>You've had a sexually transmitted infection (STI) such as chlamydia or gonorrhea.</li><li>You used a latex condom or a feminine product such as a spermicide or douche that irritated the skin of your vagina.</li><li>You left something in your vagina too long, such as a diaphragm, tampon, or <span class="qt2">cervical</span> cap, and it caused irritation.</li><li>You don't consistently use a condom when you have sex, or you have multiple sex partners.</li></ul>What are the symptoms of <span class="qt2">cervix</span> disorders?<p>You may not know that something is wrong since <span class="qt2">cervix</span> disorders may not have any symptoms. If you have symptoms, they may vary based on the <span class="qt2">cervix</span> disorder.</p><p>Symptoms can include:</p><ul><li>Vaginal bleeding that's not normal for you, such as bleeding between menstrual periods</li><li>Pain during sex or a pelvic exam</li><li>Abnormal vaginal discharge</li></ul><p>If you are pregnant, a few signs of an incompetent <span class="qt2">cervix</span> could include light vaginal bleeding, a feeling of pelvic pressure, or mild cramps. But you may not have any signs.</p>How are <span class="qt2">cervix</span> disorders diagnosed?<p>Even if you don't have symptoms, your health care provider may notice changes to the cells of your <span class="qt2">cervix</span> during a pelvic exam. Your provider may look for:</p><ul><li>Redness or inflammation (swelling) of your <span class="qt2">cervix</span> or vaginal walls</li><li>Vaginal discharge or strong odor</li></ul><p>Your provider may perform a Pap test to look for changes in your <span class="qt2">cervix</span>.</p>What are the treatments for <span class="qt2">cervix</span> disorders?<p>The treatment for <span class="qt2">cervix</span> disorders depends on the cause. It might include antibiotics or stopping using a product that causes skin irritation.</p><p>If you have had an incompetent <span class="qt2">cervix</span> in the past, you might take medicine or have ultrasound imaging tests to check how your pregnancy is going.</p>Can <span class="qt2">cervix</span> disorders be prevented?<p>You can take steps to prevent some <span class="qt2">cervix</span> disorders. This can include to:</p><ul><li>Use a condom every time you have sex. Correct usage of latex condoms greatly reduces, but does not completely eliminate, the risk of catching or spreading STIs. If you or your partner is allergic to latex, you can use polyurethane condoms.</li><li>Have regular pelvic exams.</li><li>Get tested for STIs as needed.</li><li>Avoid using personal care products that may cause skin irritation to your vagina.</li></ul></content>

      <content name="FullSummary">What is a <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">hysterectomy</span></span>?<p>A <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">hysterectomy</span></span> is surgery to remove the <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">uterus (womb). The uterus</span></span> is the place where a fetus grows during pregnancy. A <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">hysterectomy</span></span> treats problems like heavy bleeding, pain, or <span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">cancer</span></span> in the <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">uterus</span></span>.</p><p>After a <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">hysterectomy</span></span>, you no longer have menstrual periods and can't become pregnant. Sometimes the surgery also removes the ovaries and fallopian tubes. If you have both ovaries taken out,menopause symptoms will usually begin.</p>What conditions does a <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">hysterectomy</span></span> treat?<p><span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">Hysterectomy</span></span> is a major surgery. Your health care provider may suggest other treatment options first. These might include medicine, hormone therapy, or procedures to remove fibroids or stop heavy bleeding. Sometimes these won't help, or surgery might be the only option, depending on the condition that needs to be treated.</p><p>Your provider might recommend a <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">hysterectomy</span></span> if you have:</p><ul><li>Fibroids, if you are near or past menopause, have large fibroids or very heavy bleeding.</li><li>Endometriosis, that hasn't been cured by medicine or surgery.</li><li><span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">Uterine</span></span> prolapse, which can happen after several vaginal births, menopause, or because of obesity. It is when the <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">uterus</span></span> drops into the vagina.</li><li><span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">Cancer</span></span>, of the <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">uterus</span></span>, <span class="qt2">cervix</span>, ovaries, or endometrium (the lining of the <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">uterus</span></span>).</li><li>Vaginal bleeding, that is heavy or unusual and persists despite treatment.</li><li>Chronic pelvic pain, which starts in the <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">uterus. A hysterectomy</span></span> is a last resort since it doesn't fix some pelvic pain.</li><li>Adenomyosis, is a thickening of the walls of the <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">uterus. A hysterectomy</span></span> is only considered if pain is severe and no other treatments have worked.</li></ul>What are the different types of <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">hysterectomies</span></span>?<p>Your provider will discuss the type of <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">hysterectomy</span></span> you need, depending on your condition.</p><p>The different types of surgeries include:</p><ul><li>A total <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">hysterectomy</span></span> is the most common type and involves the removal of all the <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">uterus</span></span>, including the <span class="qt2">cervix</span>. The ovaries and fallopian tubes may or may not be removed.</li><li>A partial (subtotal or supracervical) <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">hysterectomy</span></span> removes just the upper part of the <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">uterus</span></span>. The <span class="qt2">cervix</span> is left in place, and your ovaries may or may not be removed</li><li>A radical <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">hysterectomy</span></span> removes all the <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">uterus</span></span>, <span class="qt2">cervix</span>, and tissue on both sides of the <span class="qt2">cervix</span> and the upper part of the vagina. This is most often used to treat certain types of <span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">cancer</span></span>, such as <span class="qt2">cervical</span> <span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">cancer</span></span>. The fallopian tubes and ovaries may or may not be removed.</li></ul>What methods are used for a <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">hysterectomy</span></span>?<p>A <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">hysterectomy</span></span> may be done several different ways. Your provider will determine the best method for the surgery based on your general health, the reason for the surgery, and other factors.</p><p>Methods to perform a <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">hysterectomy</span></span> include:</p><ul><li>Abdominal <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">hysterectomy</span></span>. A cut is made in your lower abdomen (belly). Your provider may recommend this method if you have a large <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">uterus</span></span> or to check other pelvic organs for signs of disease. This surgery has a longer recovery time than the others.</li><li>Vaginal <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">hysterectomy</span></span>. A small cut is made in your vagina. This may not be an option if you have very large fibroids.</li><li>Laparoscopic <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">hysterectomy</span></span>. Uses an instrument with a thin, lighted tube and an attached camera. This helps your provider see your pelvic organs. Small cuts are made in either your abdomen (belly) or vagina. This is not an option for all types of <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">uterine</span></span> fibroids.</li><li>Robotic surgery. Your provider guides a robotic arm to do the surgery through small cuts in your lower abdomen (belly).</li></ul><p>After a <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">hysterectomy</span></span>, it can take four to six weeks to recover, depending on the type of surgery you have.</p>What are the risks of a <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">hysterectomy</span></span>?<p>Like all surgeries, a <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">hysterectomy</span></span> has risks, even though the results are usually good. Talk to your provider about the benefits and risks of having a <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">hysterectomy</span></span>.</p><p>More serious risks can include:</p><ul><li>Too much bleeding during surgery</li><li>Infection</li><li>Blood clots</li></ul><p>Dept. of Health and Human Services Office on Women's Health</p></content>
